L:meta.interpolated.bynk - meta.embedded.comment: #90: a non-raw tagged multi-line string ("""sql) is still a Bynk string, so `\(…)` is a hole anywhere in its body — inside the embedded language's own strings and comments, and in value position (`"n": \(x)`), where that grammar's rules, not the body's top-level includes, are active. The `L:` makes the hole win over the embedded rule at the same position (JSON's invalid-escape rule). Raw r"""sql bodies carry no meta.interpolated.bynk, so they stay literal; inside a hole the exclusion stops a raw Bynk string from growing a hole. #string-escape comes first, as in #strings, so an escaped `\\(` is a backslash and a literal paren even where the embedded grammar has no escapes of its own (a SQL '…', a JS comment); Bynk decodes those escapes before the embedded language sees the text.

doc-block.comment: A doc-block closes only on a marker of its opener's length (ADR 0449), and its content is Markdown. A child begin/end rule stops the parent's end being tried, so a code fence inside the block must also end at the block's own marker; a child cannot backreference the parent's capture, hence one rule per marker length (3, 4, and 5 or more, which is approximate).

doc-fence-bynk-3.comment: A ```bynk fence in a doc-block, highlighted as Bynk. It ends on its closing fence, or just before the doc-block's own marker so the block still closes there.
doc-fence-bynk-3.name: markup.fenced_code.block.markdown

doc-fence-raw-3.comment: Any other fence in a doc-block: raw text, no Markdown inside.
doc-fence-raw-3.name: markup.fenced_code.block.markdown

doc-markdown.comment: Markdown in doc prose, from VS Code's built-in grammar. Only single-line rules: Markdown's block rules (paragraph, list, blockquote) are begin/while, which would run past the doc-block's closing marker, so list and quote markers are matched here instead. Headings are matched here too, since Markdown's own allows at most three spaces of indent and doc-blocks are often indented, with tabs among others.

doc-line.comment: #2203: a `--- text` one-line doc: three or more dashes, a space or tab, then text, first on its line. A marker alone on its line is a doc-block fence, which #doc-block matches first. An optional closer, a final run of exactly the opener's dashes after whitespace, is punctuation, not text. The text is inline Markdown.
doc-line.name: comment.line.documentation.bynk

line-comment.comment: #2203: a `//` comment, anywhere on a line.
line-comment.name: comment.line.double-slash.bynk

annotations.comment: Storage-field annotations `@ttl(…)`/`@indexed(…)`/`@retain(…)`/`@bounded(…)` (ADR 0111). Highlights the `@name` marker; the argument list is left to the ordinary number/identifier patterns.

keyword-labels.comment: #79 (bynk#2837): a reserved word names a field where it is a label, followed by `:` (`{ type: String }`, `Account { type: t, .. }`, `Push(from: …)`). The words are those #keywords and #constants colour unconditionally; a guarded contextual word (`key`, `store`, `trace`, …) is already an identifier before `:`. `::` and `:=` are not a label's colon.
keyword-labels.name: variable.other.property.bynk

keyword-members.comment: #79 (bynk#2837): a reserved word after `.` on the same line is a member: a method when a call or type arguments follow (`Sorted.from(xs)`, `fn Sorted.from(…)`), a field otherwise (`a.type`). A one-line match keeps the compiler's same-line rule; `(?<!\.)` leaves `..` and `...` alone. The words are #keyword-labels' plus `trace` and `faults`, whose guards a member can trip.

patterns.comment: `key` and `store` are CONTEXTUAL keywords (like in the parser): they introduce an agent field only in `<kw> <name>:` position, so they stay an ordinary identifier elsewhere (a `store`/`key` function parameter, a `cache.store` context). The look-ahead requires a following `<name>:` (whitespace + identifier + colon), which a parameter `store: Int` (colon adjacent) and a member `cache.store` do not match.
patterns.name: keyword.declaration.bynk

patterns.comment: State-migrations S3 (#2248): `replaces` is CONTEXTUAL after an agent's name (`agent New replaces Old {`), and `removed` before `agent` at item position (`removed agent Old`); both stay ordinary identifiers elsewhere.
patterns.name: keyword.declaration.bynk

patterns.comment: State-migrations S2 (#2224): `migrate` is a CONTEXTUAL keyword opening an agent's `migrate from N` step, highlighted only before `from`; `drop` is contextual inside a step (`drop <field>` on a line of its own), so both stay ordinary identifiers elsewhere.
patterns.name: keyword.declaration.bynk

patterns.comment: #2618: `private` is a CONTEXTUAL modifier on a `fn`, `type`, `messages`, `asset`, `embed` or `const` declaration — highlighted only immediately before one of those words, so `@cache(scope: private)` and a binding named `private` stay ordinary identifiers.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.bynk

patterns.comment: #2640: `par` is a CONTEXTUAL keyword opening a `par { … }` binding block — highlighted only before `{`, so it stays an ordinary identifier elsewhere.

patterns.comment: v0.154: `embeds` is a CONTEXTUAL keyword introducing a sum type's declared error embeddings (`embeds E as V`) — highlighted only before a type name (uppercase), so it stays an ordinary identifier elsewhere.

patterns.comment: v0.117: the observation sugar words are CONTEXTUAL keywords (parsed by lookahead, like `key`/`store`): they read as matchers only after a `Cap.op` seam reference in an `expect`. `with` is matched only when it follows `called`/`<n> times`, so an ordinary `with` identifier is left untouched; the other five are distinctive enough to highlight directly.

patterns.comment: #1706: the fault-claim word is CONTEXTUAL — `expect <call> faults` ends the line with it, so it is matched only there; an ordinary `faults` identifier mid-expression is left untouched.

patterns.comment: v0.118: the test-tier words on a `suite`/`case` header are CONTEXTUAL — a tier only after `as` (a `<name> as tier` classifier), so ordinary identifiers or `consumes … as Alias` are left untouched.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.bynk

patterns.comment: #2134: the suite/case `env { … }` clause word is CONTEXTUAL — a keyword only at the start of a line and followed by `{`, so an ordinary `env` identifier is left untouched.
v0.118: the `stub Cap.op(…) <rhs>` clause right-hand-side words — contextual, but distinctive enough (like the observation matchers) to highlight directly.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.bynk

patterns.comment: #2683: the stub latency words — `stub Cap.op(…) returns v after d` and `stub Cap.op(…) never` — contextual, so only on a `stub` line (an `after` or `never` identifier elsewhere is left untouched).
v0.117: the `trace(Cap.op)` escape hatch — a test-only builtin, matched only in call position.

strings.comment: String literals (#2619): raw multi-line, multi-line, raw (any number of `#`), and ordinary. A raw literal has no escapes and no interpolation. Order matters: `r"""` and `"""` before `"`. #2958: a multi-line literal may carry a language tag (`"""sql`). A known tag embeds that language's grammar in the body: one rule per tag, ahead of the untagged rules, since a TextMate include cannot be chosen by a capture. Any other tag is a plain string. The body is a begin/while rule that stops at the closing-delimiter line (the lexer's rule: indentation, then `"""` not followed by an identifier character or a quote), as Markdown's fenced code blocks do. The `while` is checked at every line start, even inside the embedded grammar's open rules, so an unclosed quote or bracket in the body cannot carry that language past the closing `"""`. This file is a copy of vscode-bynk's syntaxes/bynk.tmLanguage.json: change both together.

sql-strings.comment: #90: SQL's own grammar matches a one-line '…', "…" or `…` literal with a single regex, which an injection cannot break into, so a non-raw """sql body takes its strings as begin/end rules under SQL's scope names. The meta.interpolated.bynk injection then finds `\(…)` holes inside them. A doubled '' is two adjacent strings, scoped the same as one.

interpolation.comment: A `\(expr)` interpolation hole (v0.43). The escape `#string-escape` precedes this in #strings, so `\\(` (escaped backslash + paren) is a literal, not a hole.
interpolation.name: meta.embedded.interpolation.bynk

interpolation-parens.comment: Balances nested parens inside a hole so the outer `\)` only closes on the matching `)` (e.g. `\(f(x))`).

builtins.comment: Capitalised builtins must precede #types so the generic entity.name.type rule does not shadow them.
